chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
title: Why the Lunceford band was so clean and precise
summary: Crawford says the band was the cleanest he heard and credits Lunceford's discipline, Sy Oliver and Willie Smith.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Now, you were telling me about the clarity of the
band, since I spoke to you last, that you had listened to some recordings of the Lunceford band again.
And would you like to go into some of the --
Elaborate a little bit on it.

I would love to. You know, I laid off from listening to the band, and I hear all this avant garde guys. But that Lunceford band, without a doubt, bar none, was the cleanest band I've heard of all of them. And I got so engrossed in it the other day, when my wife was playing it for me, until I just -- every number she played was so clean, so precise, that reed section, you couldn't beat them. That includes Duke's section and all the rest of them. Rhythm section, yeah, you had better drummers, better bass players, perhaps, but when it came down to the rhythm section, they were just in there. Maybe a little heavy at times, maybe a little punctuated too much, but all in all, that whole entire band was so precise. I enjoyed it.
How did you all get the kind of discipline that it took for that kind of cleanness to come out of the band?
Well, Jimmy Lunceford was the main man. He was the leader, he was the teacher of discipline and

whatnot. But I have to give credit where it's due. That Sy Oliver got in there and Willie Smith, yes, he arranged. But all of them had to just take their hats off to Sy Oliver. Sy Melvin Oliver never (inaudible). That man, he really was the instigator of all the precision work and just played his arrangements. And he'd get pretty burned up, too, at times. If you didn't do it right. But Willie Smith, without a doubt, would get very horrified with any saxophone player there -- Jack Carruthers, Joe Thomas, Willie Smith, any of them in that band. They didn't play the way it hit with him, oh, he wouldn't speak to you. He'd just let the whole thing go.

Now, if you want me to conduct? Tell these fellows that they have to play the way I'm playing. Oh, he was the living end (inaudible) and all of them popping right together. And Lunceford, so clean, dible), the question you asked me, Lunceford was the one that established discipline in that band.
Do you think it had anything to do with his educational background, with him having --

Without a doubt. The man was a leader. Duke Ellington was a leader, but not the type that Lunceford was. That's why they wanted to break that band up when we first hit New York. They wouldn't let us in the union. Finally got in there, I mean, I did, and all the guys that couldn't cut it the way it was supposed to be cut, they fell by the wayside, Stanley.
